$comment: What the human brain tends to like, from empirical aesthetics research. Shared by every approach. 'strength' is our reading of the evidence: strong = replicated or meta-analysed; moderate = solid studies, some limits; contested = mixed results. Style scores at the bottom are our synthesis, not a published ranking.

findings.title: Curves over sharp angles
findings.finding: People prefer objects and patterns with curved contours to sharp-angled ones; sharp angles may read as a possible threat.
findings.effect: Meta-analysis of 61 studies: medium effect (Hedges' g = 0.39). Reliable, not universal; depends on presentation time, stimulus type, expertise and task.
findings.designRule: Default to organic shapes and rounded corners; use sharp points only deliberately.
sources: Chuquichambi et al. (2022), Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences 1518

findings.title: Low visual complexity
findings.finding: Websites with low visual complexity and high prototypicality were rated most appealing; complexity is judged within 17-50 ms, before people can read anything.
findings.effect: Complexity affects ratings even at 17 ms exposure; high complexity lowers beauty ratings even for familiar layouts.
findings.designRule: One focal point, few elements, generous space. Complexity is the first thing the eye judges.
sources: Tuch et al. (2012), International Journal of Human-Computer Studies 70(11)

findings.title: Easy to process feels good
findings.finding: Features that make a stimulus easier to perceive (clarity, contrast, symmetry, figure-ground separation, repetition, prototypicality) tend to increase liking.
findings.effect: A theory with broad support across many studies, reviewed by Reber, Schwarz and Winkielman.
findings.designRule: High contrast between figure and ground, clear silhouettes, familiar structure, repeated system elements.
sources: Reber, Schwarz & Winkielman (2004), Personality and Social Psychology Review 8(4)

findings.title: The 50 ms first impression
findings.finding: People rate the visual appeal of a web page consistently after seeing it for only 50 ms.
findings.effect: Ratings at 50 ms correlated highly with ratings at 500 ms. Shows speed of judgement; it does not measure whether people stay or buy.
findings.designRule: The silhouette, colour and focal point must work before anyone reads a word.
sources: Lindgaard et al. (2006), Behaviour & Information Technology 25

findings.title: Familiar, with a twist (MAYA)
findings.finding: Typicality and novelty jointly predict preference: people like new designs as long as the novelty does not cost typicality, and vice versa ('Most Advanced, Yet Acceptable').
findings.effect: Both factors contributed about equally across three studies, and suppressed each other when considered alone; expertise did not change the balance.
findings.designRule: Keep the format recognisable (a poster looks like a poster) and put the surprise in one place: the idea.
sources: Hekkert, Snelders & van Wieringen (2003), British Journal of Psychology 94

findings.title: Nature's mid-range complexity
findings.finding: Across natural scenes, simulated coastlines and Pollock paintings, people preferred statistical fractals with dimension D = 1.3-1.5 over smoother (1.1-1.2) or rougher (1.6-1.9) ones.
findings.effect: Consistent across image sources, not explained by density. Later work found individual differences and sub-groups, so 'universal' is contested.
findings.designRule: Organic detail should be moderately rough, like a coastline or a hand-drawn line: not ruler-smooth, not noisy.
sources: Spehar, Clifford, Newell & Taylor (2003), Computers & Graphics 27
Street et al. (2016) and Spehar, Walker & Taylor (2016), Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 10

findings.title: Handmade signals care
findings.finding: Products described as handmade are seen as more attractive, mainly because they are felt to symbolically contain love.
findings.effect: Four studies; strongest when the product expresses love (e.g. gifts for close people).
findings.designRule: Visible human marks (a wobbling line, a cut edge) add warmth; keep them deliberate and consistent.
sources: Fuchs, Schreier & van Osselaer (2015), Journal of Marketing 79(2)

findings.title: Colours borrow feelings from things
findings.finding: Colour preference follows how people feel about objects of that colour: blues (clear sky, clean water) are among the most liked; browns and dark yellows or olives (rot, waste) among the least.
findings.effect: Object associations explained about 80% of the variance in average colour preference in the original data. Culture and context shift associations.
findings.designRule: Pick ground colours whose everyday associations suit the product; avoid muddy browns and olives as large fields unless the product's world makes them positive (coffee, bread, wood).

findings.title: Beautiful looks easier to use
findings.finding: Interfaces rated more attractive were also perceived as easier to use.
findings.effect: An early, influential study; the perception effect is well known, but it is about perceived, not actual, usability.
findings.designRule: Craft is not decoration: polish raises trust in clarity.

myths.reality: Evidence is weak and inconsistent. Fechner's 1876 rectangle test found a modest lean; later work found no reliable effect in real artworks, strong individual differences (McManus), and no implicit preference (Swami & Stieger, 2015).
myths.useInstead: Use proportions that suit the format and the grid; don't justify a layout by the golden ratio.

myths.claim: Each colour causes a fixed emotion (red = hunger, blue = trust).
myths.reality: Colour preference is driven largely by learned associations with objects and context (Palmer & Schloss, 2010), so meanings change with culture and product.
myths.useInstead: Choose colours by what they are associated with in the product's own world, then test.

styles.$comment: Our synthesis: each style family scored 0-2 on how strongly it typically uses each evidence-backed feature. Not a published ranking. Preference is not the only goal: polarising styles can win attention and memorability.

list.name: Humanist Minimal
list.summary: Hand ink line, organic paper shapes, one idea, lots of space.
list.watch: Can drift into cute; Wada pairs vary in contrast.

list.name: Mid-century Modern
list.summary: 1950s-60s optimism: kidney and boomerang shapes, starbursts, flat colour, simplified nature illustration (think Charley Harper, Eames).
list.watch: Nostalgia can read as pastiche; keep it fresh (MAYA).

list.name: Biophilic Organic
list.summary: Leaves, water, branching growth, natural textures and sky and plant colours.
list.watch: Busy detail costs clarity; stock-nature clichés.

list.name: Soft Modern UI
list.summary: Rounded cards, generous space, calm blues and light tints, clean sans type.

list.name: Modern Clarity (Swiss)
list.summary: Strict grid, big sans type, flat colour, objective photography.
list.watch: Clear but cold; angles and hard edges.

list.name: Editorial Classic
list.summary: Serif headlines, columns, rules and photography, like a magazine.

list.name: Maximalist / Memphis
list.summary: Pattern on pattern, many colours, playful clutter.
list.watch: High complexity lowers average liking; polarising, memorable.

list.name: Brutalist
list.summary: Raw blocks, default fonts, hard borders, deliberate roughness.
list.watch: Rejects fluency on purpose; works for niche, attention-seeking brands.
